quotes.quote: Found only in the blackwater swamps near Kota Kerincikiri, on the Indonesian island of Sumatra.

sections.html:
• Genus Parosphromenus (licorice gouramis).
  • IUCN Red List: Critically Endangered (extremely high risk of extinction in the wild).
  • Origin: wild caught.
  • Described in 2012.

Parosphromenus phoenicurus, the red-finned licorice gourami, was described in 2012. It is known only from a single blackwater swamp near Langgam, in the Sungai Kampar drainage about 40 km southeast of Pekanbaru, Riau, Sumatra. Horst Linke found it in 2008, and it was traded as "sp. Langgam" until it was named. The name means "crimson tail".
Blackwater swamp measured at 27°C, pH 5.25 and only 7 µS/cm conductivity.
Keep a group of 5 in 20 litres or larger, or a pair for breeding.
Micropredator. It only eats live food. Suitable foods include live baby brine shrimp, daphnia and blackworms.
Peaceful, but males can be territorial. It can share a tank with tiny, calm blackwater fish such as Boraras. Never mix different Parosphromenus species, since they can hybridize.

Body elongated and slightly compressed. Diamond-shaped caudal fin with an almost triangular black patch; turquoise pelvic fins with black filaments. Males have much more colourful and longer fins than females. In males, the dorsal and anal fins run from a black base through a bright crimson band, a narrow iridescent blue band and a black band to a light blue edge. Aquarium-bred males show more red than wild fish. It is told apart from the similar bintan and harveyi types by the bold black and red bands on its unpaired fins. Parosphromenus tweediei is its closest relative but has a rounded tail. Maximum size is 2.9 cm for wild fish; aquarium-bred fish reach 4 cm.

Cave spawner with a head-down courtship, like its relatives. Match the very low conductivity of its home water. Breeding has become harder since the first captive successes, and only a few small breeding stocks exist.
